day-1.t: Day 1 — Why a list beats followers

b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand the difference between an audience you rent and one you own
Choose what you will send and how often
Write down the one action you want from your list

b.v: About 15 minutes. No tools needed today. Just decisions.

A Facebook follower sees your post if the platform decides to show it. An email address or a WhatsApp number that someone gave you on purpose is yours to contact. That is why a list of 400 real customers can outsell 4,000 followers.
1) Rented versus owned

v: Rented audience = followers on a platform. Reach changes when the platform changes its rules.
Owned audience = email addresses and phone numbers given to you with permission
Both are useful. The owned list is what survives a bad month for the platform.
A list is not a download. It is a group of people who expect to hear from you.

b.v: 2) Decide what you will send
People stay on a list for one of three reasons: useful information, a good price, or because they like you. Choose your main reason now, because it decides who you invite.

Choose one main job:|Useful: tips and reminders, such as seasonal care for the machine you sold|Offers: early access and discounts for regular buyers|Relationship: stories from the shop, new stock, behind the counter|Then write one sentence: 'I will send ___ about ___ , ___ times a month.'
Example for a Lahore bike workshop: 'I will send one message a month with a service reminder and one small maintenance tip, plus early notice of any parts sale.' Clear, useful, easy to keep.
3) One action, repeated
Every message should ask for one thing. Reply, tap a link, order, or visit. Two asks halve the response to each.

Do not build a list by adding every number in your phone contacts or scraping emails from groups. That is not a list; it is a complaint waiting to happen, and it can get your email account or WhatsApp number restricted. Permission is the foundation, not the paperwork.
Practice

Do this now:|Write your one sentence: what you will send, and how often|Write the single action you want most|List the three things your customers always ask about. Those are your first three messages.|Decide which channel suits your customers more: email, WhatsApp, or both

day-2.t: Day 2 — Build a list the honest way

b.v: Today's goal

v: Create one clear place where people can join
Write a sign-up reason worth giving a number for
Set up the confirmation step that keeps lists clean

b.v: About 25 minutes. You will set up one form and one welcome message today.
A list grows from one thing: an offer of value in exchange for permission. 'Join our newsletter' is not value. 'Get 5 percent off your first order and a message when new stock arrives' is value.
1) Where people join

v: A form on your website, in the footer and on the product page
A WhatsApp link in your Instagram bio, so people start the chat themselves
A QR code on the counter, the receipt or the parcel
At checkout, with a clear unticked box", "In person, after a good conversation, with the customer typing their own number

b.v: 2) Write the sign-up line
Three parts: what they get, how often, and that they can leave. Say it in one short line.

@Text
WEAK:
Subscribe to our newsletter.

WORKING:
Get new stock photos and prices on WhatsApp before we post them publicly.
One message a week. Reply STOP any time to leave.
[Your name] [Your number]
The working version is specific about the benefit, honest about frequency, and states the exit. Those three details increase sign-ups and reduce complaints at the same time.
3) Confirm, then welcome

Double opt-in means the person clicks a link or sends a message to confirm. It feels like extra work, but it removes wrong numbers and people who never meant to join, which protects your sender reputation.

Set it up:|Create a simple form with two fields: name and email or number|Turn on confirmation, so they must confirm before joining|Send the welcome message immediately after confirming|Keep the form on one page, with no menu and no clutter|Test it yourself with a different email or number

Do not pre-tick the consent box at checkout, and do not buy an email list. Bought lists are full of people who never heard of you. They mark you as spam, and your future messages start landing in the junk folder for everyone, including real customers.
Practice

Do this now:|Write your sign-up line using the three parts|Put the form or WhatsApp link in one visible place today|Send yourself a test sign-up and read what arrives|Fix anything confusing in that first message
Today's goal

v: Write three welcome messages that run automatically
Give value before asking for money
Set the expectation of how often you write

b.v: About 25 minutes. This is the highest-return writing you will do for your list.

A welcome sequence is a short set of messages sent automatically to a new subscriber. New subscribers are the most interested they will ever be, so this is when they read everything. Most small businesses send nothing and lose that moment.
1) Three messages, three jobs

v: Message 1, immediately = thank you, what to expect, and one useful thing
Message 2, next day = the story and the proof. Who you are, why they can trust you.
Message 3, day three = the offer, once, without pressure

b.v: 2) Write it plainly
Short messages work better than long ones. One idea, one link, one action. Write like a message to a customer you know, not like a company announcement.

@Email
Subject: Your Rs 300 off, and one tip before you buy

Assalam o alaikum {{first_name}},

Thank you for joining. Here is the code: WELCOME300, valid for 30 days on any order above Rs 2,000.

One tip first, because it saves people money: always check the stitching on the inside seam before you wash a new suit. If it is loose, one stitch now saves a tear later.

I send one message a week: new stock, prices, and one useful tip. Nothing else.

Reply to this email if you have a question. A real person reads it.

Ali
Malik Fabrics, Lahore
Why it works: the subject names the benefit, the code is real, the tip is useful even if they never buy, the frequency is stated, and a reply is invited.
3) Set it and check it

Build the sequence:|Create three messages in your email tool or as saved WhatsApp replies|Set message 1 to send immediately, 2 after one day, 3 after three days|Use the person's name if your tool supports it, and test that it fills correctly|Send the whole sequence to yourself and read it as a customer|Fix the typos, then turn it on

Do not put the hard sell in the first message before giving anything. Also do not promise a discount you will not honour, or set a sequence to send five emails in three days. New subscribers leave fastest when they feel pushed.
Practice

Do this now:|Write the three messages, each under 150 words|Include one real code or one real useful tip|Set the timing|Send the sequence to yourself|Ask one friend to read it and say where they would stop reading
Today's goal

v: Write a subject line that earns the open
Structure a short message with one clear action
Build a repeatable monthly rhythm

b.v: About 20 minutes. You will write one real newsletter today and send it this week.
A newsletter is a regular message with something worth reading. It is not a catalogue. The goal is to stay remembered so that when the customer needs your product, your name comes first.
1) The subject line
The subject decides whether the message is opened at all. Specific and short beats clever. Avoid words that look like spam, such as FREE!!! or 100% GUARANTEED.

v: Specific: 'New lawn stock, Rs 3,850, 4 colours'
Useful: 'One thing to check before you store winter clothes'
Personal: 'A small change to our delivery days'
Weak: 'Our latest newsletter', 'Exciting news!', 'Don't miss out!!!'

b.v: 2) A structure you can keep

Write in this order:|One line about something real, such as new stock or a customer story|One useful tip related to what you sell|One offer or update, clearly priced|One action: reply, order, or visit|Sign with a human name and the shop
Keep it under 200 words. Most people read on a phone between two other tasks. A short message that gets read beats a beautiful one that gets deleted.
3) A rhythm you can hold
Monthly is enough for most small shops. Weekly works if you have new stock every week. Pick a day and keep it, because people start to expect it, and expectation is the whole point.

Plan one month:|Week 1: new stock or a restock announcement|Week 2: a tip, no selling|Week 3: one offer with a real deadline|Week 4: a customer story or a question answered|Write the four subjects now, so the month is half done

Do not send the same newsletter to your email list and as a WhatsApp broadcast without adjusting it. Email can carry a long link; WhatsApp cannot, and long forwarded text looks like spam. Rewrite for the channel.
Practice

Do this now:|Write four subject lines for next month|Write this month's newsletter in under 200 words|Include one real price and one real action|Send it to yourself first, open it on your phone|Fix anything that looks cramped, then send it to your list

day-5.t: Day 5 — Offers without burning the list

b.v: Today's goal

v: Plan offers that do not train people to wait
Use deadlines honestly
Segment so you stop discounting to your best customers

b.v: About 20 minutes. Bring last month's numbers. Offers need maths, not excitement.
A list that gets a discount every week becomes a list that only buys at a discount. Worse, your full price stops looking real. Offers should be events with a reason, not a permanent state.
1) Reasons that are true

v: Season: Eid stock arriving, winter ending
Stock: last two pieces of a design, honestly counted
Anniversary: three years in this shop
New: first look at a new line for list members
Clearance: a colour or size that did not sell

b.v: Notice that none of these is invented. A reason makes the offer believable, and believability is what keeps your price intact afterwards.
2) Design one offer properly

Build it on paper:|What exactly is included|The normal price and the offer price|Your profit after the offer. If it is negative, change the offer.|The deadline, in a date and time|Who gets it: everyone, or only a group|What happens after the deadline, in writing

Example, illustrative: a Karachi bakery has 40 boxes of dates to move before the season ends. Cost is Rs 900 a box. Normal price Rs 1,600. They offer two boxes for Rs 2,600 to list members for four days. Profit stays positive per box and the stock clears before it becomes a loss.
3) Segment before you discount
Sending a discount to people who buy at full price is giving away money. Split your list into three simple groups and treat them differently.

v: New = joined in the last 30 days. Give the welcome offer once.
Repeat = bought two or more times. Give early access, not discounts.
Quiet = no order in six months. This is where a real offer belongs.

b.v: Do not run a countdown that resets, or say 'today only' and repeat it tomorrow. Customers notice, and your future deadlines become meaningless. A fake deadline is a small lie that costs a large amount of trust.
Practice

Do this now:|Pick one true reason for an offer this month|Write the four numbers: cost, normal price, offer price, profit|Write the deadline as a date and time|Split your list into new, repeat and quiet|Send the offer only to the group it fits

day-6.t: Day 6 — Landing in the inbox, not the junk folder

b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand what deliverability means
Fix the four things that send you to spam
Set up the technical basics once

b.v: About 25 minutes. Some of this may need one message to your web person.
Deliverability is whether your message arrives in the inbox or in spam, or nowhere at all. You can write a perfect email that nobody ever sees. The causes are mostly technical and mostly fixable.
1) The four causes

v: A bought or scraped list = many strangers marking you as spam
No authentication = your domain has not proved it is allowed to send
Image only messages with no real text = filters cannot read them, so they look suspicious
Too many links and shouting = repeated FREE!!! CLICK NOW patterns

b.v: 2) The technical basics
Three records in your domain settings prove you are the real sender. Your hosting company or email tool can add them for you.

Ask your provider for these:|SPF, which lists the servers allowed to send for your domain|DKIM, which signs your messages so tampering is visible|DMARC, which tells receiving servers what to do when checks fail|A real reply address that a human reads|A physical address or city in the footer, so you are identifiable

If you send from a free Gmail account to a few dozen customers, these records are handled by Google. If you send from your own domain through a tool, you need them set up. Ask once and keep the reply.
3) Habits that keep you in the inbox

Every send:|Use a plain subject line with no ALL CAPS|Write at least a few lines of real text, not only an image|Keep one main link, and make the link text say where it goes|Send to people who expect it, not to a purchased list|Remove hard bounces and complaints immediately|Send at a steady rhythm instead of 2,000 messages after six quiet months

Never send a test campaign to a big list 'to see what happens'. Reputation is built slowly and lost in one send. Also do not use a shared free inbox for bulk mail: providers limit daily sends, and a restriction can lock you out of your normal email too.
Practice

Do this now:|Ask your email tool whether SPF, DKIM and DMARC are set for your domain|Check your last campaign: was it image heavy or text heavy?|Rewrite one subject line without capital letters or exclamation marks|Send a test to three different addresses, including a Gmail and an Outlook|Ask where it landed: inbox, promotions tab, or spam

day-7.t: Day 7 — Consent, unsubscribe and the rules

b.v: Today's goal

v: Understand what consent means in practice
Make leaving easy and immediate
Know which records to keep

b.v: About 20 minutes. This lesson protects the business, so read it twice.

Rules about email and messaging differ by country and change over time. This lesson gives the principles that almost every system expects, but you must check the rules that apply where you and your customers are. When unsure, ask a lawyer or a business adviser; do not guess with other people's data.
1) What consent looks like
Consent means the person agreed, knowingly, to receive marketing from you, and can show it. Silence is not consent. A phone number given for a delivery is not consent to marketing.

v: Clear: the person ticked a box or sent you a message asking to join
Specific: they agreed to marketing messages, not just to a receipt
Recorded: you can say when and how they agreed
Withdrawable: they can leave at any time, easily

b.v: 2) The unsubscribe line
Every marketing email needs a way out. Every WhatsApp broadcast needs a plain instruction. Make it one tap, not a form.

Get this right:|Put 'Reply STOP to leave' in every WhatsApp broadcast|Use your email tool's built-in unsubscribe link, which works without a login|Honour the request the same day, not next month|Keep a suppression list of people who left, so you never add them again by accident|Do not ask why they left before you remove them. Remove first, ask later.
3) Records worth keeping
If a customer complains, you need to show how they joined. A simple sheet is enough for a small shop.

Keep a consent log with:|Name and email or number|Date and place of consent, such as 'shop counter' or 'website form'|What they agreed to receive|Date they left, if they left|Where the record is stored, and who can see it

Do not sell, rent or share your list with anyone, and do not add a customer to a group where their number is visible to strangers. That is a privacy problem and, in some places, a legal one. If you are unsure what the law requires for your business, get local advice rather than copying another shop's wording.
Practice

Do this now:|Check your last email: is there a working unsubscribe link?|Add 'Reply STOP to leave' to your WhatsApp broadcast template|Create a consent sheet with the five columns above|Add today's new contacts with the date and place they agreed|Write down one question to ask a local adviser about your situation

day-8.t: Day 8 — WhatsApp Business without annoying people

b.v: Today's goal

v: Set up the business profile and catalogue properly
Send broadcasts that feel personal
Know when to move a chat to a call or a visit

b.v: About 20 minutes. Do this on your phone; it is a phone business.

In Pakistan, WhatsApp is often the whole shop: catalogue, price list, order desk and delivery updates. The advantage is speed and trust. The danger is that a careless broadcast gets your number reported and restricted.
1) Set the shop up

Do this in WhatsApp Business:|Business name, category and a real photo or logo|Description: what you sell, city, delivery areas, hours|Catalogue with at least five items, each with a photo and price|Away message for after hours, saying when you will reply|Greeting message that asks what they need, not a wall of text|Quick replies for price, delivery, size and payment
2) Broadcasts with permission
A broadcast sends one message to many people privately. It is powerful and it is easy to abuse. Only include people who asked to hear from you.

v: Ask once, clearly: 'Should I send you new stock photos every week?'
Keep the list small and interested, not large and cold
One broadcast a week at most for most shops
Always include how to leave
Never add people from groups without asking

b.v: Example of a broadcast that works: 'New stock in this morning: 4 lawn designs, Rs 3,850 each. Photos in the catalogue. Reply with the design number and your city. Reply STOP to leave the list.' Short, priced, one action, clear exit.
3) Close the sale in the chat

When someone asks about an item:|Reply within minutes during business hours|Send the price, two photos of the actual piece and the delivery time|Ask for the one detail you need, such as size or colour|Confirm the total, including delivery, in one line|Send a payment request or your JazzCash or Easypaisa detail clearly|Send the tracking or a photo before dispatch|Ask for a review after delivery

Do not send 'Dear customer, our new collection is here' to 500 people at once. It reads as spam, it gets reported, and reports can restrict your number. Write like a shopkeeper: short, specific, priced. Also never ask a customer to send money to a personal account without a clear written record of what they are buying.
Practice

Do this now:|Complete your business profile and catalogue|Add three quick replies|Write one broadcast with a price and a STOP line|Send it to a small test list of five willing customers|Note how many reply and what they ask

day-9.t: Day 9 — Measure opens, clicks and actual sales

b.v: Today's goal

v: Read the three numbers that matter
Understand why open rates are only a hint
Tie messages to real money in your order book

b.v: About 20 minutes. Use a laptop if you can; the reports are easier to read wide.
Reports can flatter you. An open is not a read, a click is not an order, and a WhatsApp reply is not a sale. Measure all three levels, and trust the last one.
1) The three levels

v: Delivered = it reached the inbox or the phone. Low delivery means a list or technical problem.
Opened or read = a weak signal. Privacy features and image blocking make it unreliable.
Clicked or replied = a real sign of interest. This is the number to improve first.
Ordered = the only number that pays the bills

b.v: 2) Link and code tracking without spyware
You do not need advanced tracking. Two simple habits connect messages to money: a unique code per campaign, and one link per message.

Set this up:|Use a code such as EID25 for one campaign only|Ask customers to mention the code when they order|Use one trackable link, such as a product page or a WhatsApp click link|Record in your order book which code or message brought the order|Every month, add up revenue per campaign and compare to the effort
3) Read a month of results
One number means nothing. The pattern over a month tells you what to change.
Every month write five lines:|Messages sent|Delivered and opened, roughly|Clicks or replies|Orders and rupees received|What I will change next month, one thing only

Do not judge a campaign by opens alone. A message with a beautiful subject and no orders is a failure even at a high open rate. And do not compare your open rate to a blog post you read: tools, lists and industries differ, so compare only your own months to each other.
Practice

Do this now:|Create a code for your next campaign|Add a column to your order book for the code|Send one message with the code and one link|At the end of the week, count replies and orders|Write one sentence on what the numbers tell you

day-10.t: Day 10 — List hygiene and a routine that lasts

b.v: Today's goal

v: Clean your list of dead and wrong contacts
Run a monthly 30-minute routine
Decide when to ask people to leave

b.v: About 20 minutes. Then put the routine in your calendar and keep it.
A list with many dead addresses hurts you: providers see low engagement and start sending everything to spam. Cleaning feels like shrinking, but it raises the number of people who actually see you.
1) Clean quarterly

v: Hard bounce = the address does not exist. Remove it immediately.
Soft bounce = full inbox or temporary problem. Keep for a while, then remove.
Complaint = someone pressed spam. Remove and never re-add.
Inactive = no open or click for six months. Try one re-engagement message, then remove.
Wrong number = a stranger replies. Apologise, remove at once.

b.v: Do this once every three months:|Export the list with the last activity date|Remove every hard bounce and complaint|Send one short re-engagement message to the quiet group|Remove those who still do not respond|Write the new total and the date
2) The monthly routine

Thirty minutes, same day each month:|Write and send the newsletter|Check delivery and complaints|Clean any bounces|Add the month's numbers to your five line report|Plan next month's four subjects|Check that the consent sheet is up to date
3) Know when to stop
Some people will never buy. Keeping them costs you deliverability and teaches you nothing. It is better to have 600 engaged readers than 3,000 addresses that ignore you.
Also be willing to end a channel that does not fit your customers. If nobody in your market reads email but everyone answers WhatsApp, put your effort there and keep email for receipts and records.

Do not keep adding people to the list after they leave, and do not move an unsubscribed person to a new tool to 'start fresh'. That breaks the promise you made and, in many places, the law. A small honest list is an asset; a large dishonest one is a liability.
Practice

Finish with this:|Clean your list today: remove bounces and complaints|Send one re-engagement message to quiet contacts|Set a repeating monthly reminder for the routine|Write your target for next month: orders from messages|Check the number on the same day next month, not before
